terms.grammar: impersonal: habet stands for rēs sē habet, “the thing holds well”
evidence: Cic. Mur. 14: bene habet: jacta sunt fundāmenta dēfēnsiōnis (Lewis & Short), s.v. bene
Hor. S. 2.6.4: bene est. nīl amplius ōrō
Cic. Att. 1.7: apud mātrem rēctē est, she is quite well (Lewis & Short), s.v. regō
Traupman p. 98: rēctē est, everything’s fine
terms.comment: Of people, it says they are well: apud mātrem rēctē est, all is well at your mother’s.

phrases.english: it is good. I ask for nothing more

sources: Lewis & Short: bene · Lewis & Short: habeo · Lewis & Short: recte
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 98, checked against the searchable text and the page image (12 November 2026).
Hor. S. 2.6.4 from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-horatius), checked against the edition named there.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
